title: IonQ speeds engineering simulation with quantum computing
excerpt: IonQ and Synopsys demonstrate a hybrid quantum approach that cuts engineering simulation runtimes by up to 14.6%.
content:
News | September 22, 2026

By Asma Adhimi



IonQ and Synopsys have demonstrated a hybrid quantum computing approach that reduced the runtime of large-scale engineering simulations by as much as 14.6%. The work integrates a quantum algorithm into a conventional computer-aided engineering workflow used for applications including automotive crash analysis and jet engine simulation.

For eeNews Europe readers, the results offer a practical example of how quantum processors could be inserted into existing industrial software rather than replacing classical computing outright. They also point to near-term opportunities for reducing compute time, energy use and infrastructure costs in simulation-heavy engineering workloads.

Quantum targets simulation bottleneck

Engineering simulations can involve systems with hundreds of millions of variables, placing heavy demands on high-performance computing clusters. Before those systems can be solved, software must organize the underlying equations efficiently to minimize unnecessary calculations and memory usage.

IonQ and Synopsys integrated a quantum algorithm into Synopsys’s Ansys LS-DYNA simulation workflow to optimize this reordering step. Rather than relying solely on conventional trial-and-error methods, the quantum component was used to identify arrangements intended to reduce computational overhead.

“Engineering simulations for jet engines or automotive crash tests require extremely large classical compute clusters running for days at a time. By embedding an advanced quantum algorithm into the core workflow, we reduced total simulation times by up to 14.6 percent,” said Dr. Martin Roetteler, IonQ’s Vice President of Quantum Solutions and Technical Fellow and co-author of the paper. “Because this complex organizing step only needs to happen once at the start of a simulation, the time saved pays off repeatedly. That means faster solutions, reduced compute costs, and lower energy consumption for industrial users.”

Tested on industrial-scale models

The researchers tested the hybrid workflow on digital models including an automobile, industrial drill component, fluid impeller and jet engine assembly. The largest meshes contained up to 35 million data points.

Numerical simulations used up to 150 qubits, while physical execution was validated on IonQ’s 36-qubit Forte trapped-ion quantum computer. Across the tested models, runtime improvements were at least 5.9%, with the largest reduction reaching 14.6%.

According to the companies, a simulation that would normally require seven days on a classical supercomputer could therefore save roughly one day of computing time under comparable conditions.

Near-term hybrid quantum focus

“Together with IonQ, we are advancing the development of quantum computers and hybrid simulation workloads to unlock new possibilities for engineering design and optimization,” said Prith Banerjee, Senior Vice President of Innovation at Synopsys. “Quantum computers have the potential to drastically accelerate large simulation workloads while improving predictive accuracy. By focusing on achievable breakthroughs in the NISQ era, we can unlock some of that potential in the near-term for our customers while preparing for the full promise of fault-tolerant quantum computing.”

The paper, “End-to-end Performance of Quantum-Accelerated Large-Scale Linear Algebra Workflows,” received a 1st Place Best Paper Award at IEEE Quantum Week 2026 in Toronto and was one of nine IonQ papers accepted for the event.
